Fall 2026 · CEET 234A · MWF

**Instructor:** Jesse Kinder, Professor of Physics
**Office:** SE 214, or SE 204 (open study/group-work space)
**Office hours:** Mon/Wed 3:30–5:30 p.m., Tue/Thu 4:30–5:30 p.m.
**Text:** *Six Ideas That Shaped Physics*, Thomas A. Moore — Units C (Conservation Laws) and N
(Newton's Laws), 4th edition (3rd edition is fine).

## Format

This is a studio course: lecture and lab are one class, not two. Physics education research is
consistent on one point — you learn physics by doing it, not by watching someone talk about it —
so most of our time together is discussion, problem solving, and hands-on lab work. Come
prepared: read the assigned section *before* class, and bring pencil, paper, and a calculator
(laptop/tablet welcome too).

**A typical class:**

- Your questions (~10 min)
- Quick problems, key ideas (~20 min)
- Group work on a Rich Context problem (~30 min)
- Lab activity (~60 min)

## Grading

Grades shouldn't get in the way of learning, so this course doesn't run on point totals. There
are three tiers: **Fail**, **Pass** (with an argued grade of D, C, or B), and **Mastery (A)**.

**To pass**, you need all of:

- 6 labs and lab memos completed satisfactorily
- Problem-solving evidence from 6 chapters in each unit
- 60% or higher on both unit quizzes (Canvas, open book/note, retake as often as you want
  through Week 10 — only your best score counts)

**If you pass**, you argue your own grade — D, C, or B — from the evidence in your portfolio:
effort, progress, and mastery over the term. Rough guide: D is minimal effort and progress; C is
good, regular effort with most work complete; B is strong, consistent effort with a complete,
well-organized portfolio.

**For an A**, you additionally need to pass an A-level exam — a chalk talk or written exam,
entirely optional, scheduled during office hours — for each unit. These test whether you can
think like a physicist under pressure, not whether you can do algebra. You can attempt them more
than once.

## Portfolio

Everything you do for this class — problem solving, group work, lab memos, data and analysis,
grade reflections — goes in your portfolio, a folder shared with you on OneDrive. This is where
your case for a grade comes from, so keep it current, not reconstructed in Week 10.

## Contact

Grades, assignments, and quizzes live on Canvas.

## Academic Integrity

Work with others, use outside resources, learn from peers — but submit your own original work.
Presenting someone else's work as your own undermines the portfolio system this course runs on:
it stops being *evidence of your learning*. Confirmed plagiarism or cheating means the work in
question doesn't count as portfolio evidence, and reporting to the Student Affairs Office is
required regardless. Review Oregon Tech's
[Student Academic Integrity Policy](https://www.oit.edu/sites/default/files/document/student-academic-integrity-policy.pdf)
if you're not already familiar with it.

## Accessibility

If you need accommodation because of a disability, contact me at the start of the term and reach
out to [Disability Services](http://www.oit.edu/academics/ssc/disability-services) — we rely on
them to coordinate accommodations.
